lineages.name: Donga and the Tia Ciata circle
lineages.why: 'Pelo Telefone', registered by Donga with Mauro de Almeida and recorded by Baiano for Odeon in 1917, is counted as the first recorded samba; it was a collective creation from a candomblé house, involving Pixinguinha and João da Baiana among others.

lineages.name: Cartola
lineages.why: Co-founded Mangueira in 1928, disappeared in the 1940s and was rediscovered washing cars in 1956. He wrote slower, contemplative sambas with tritone substitutions and uncommon modulations — over 500 songs — and made his first solo album at 66 in 1974.

lineages.name: Paulinho da Viola
lineages.why: Raised among choro masters (his father a guitarist; Pixinguinha and Jacob do Bandolim around the house), he writes traditional sambas with sophisticated harmony and a soft voice, released about an album a year in the 1970s, and wrote carnival sambas for schools.

lineages.name: Fundo de Quintal and Beth Carvalho
lineages.why: Beth Carvalho championed pagode from 1978, recording its pioneers including Zeca Pagodinho; Fundo de Quintal fixed the pagode sound in the early 1980s with banjo, tan-tan and hand repique, and carried partido alto forward.

name: Samba

notes.text: Three surdos carry the pulse: the segunda (higher) plays beat 1, the primeira (lowest, 22–26 inch) plays beat 2 — the strongest point of the bar and the whole bateria's reference — and the terceira (cortador) cuts across both with fills and syncopations and is the only surdo with room to improvise.

Above the surdos, tamborim, pandeiro, caixa, agogô and ganzá interlock on a continuous sixteenth-note subdivision, with accents that dance around the pulse rather than landing on it; on a kit this is condensed into bass drum, snare, hi-hat and cross-stick.
The syncopated samba that emerged from the Estácio neighbourhood in the late 1920s — the surdo figure its musicians sang as 'bum bum paticumbum pugurumdum' — is the rhythm carnival samba is built on.

Carnival tempos rose as schools grew: about 115–120 BPM in 1972, over 130 by 1987, over 150 by 2004 — at which point each beat is filled with plain eighths because the syncopation can no longer be played. Recent schools have deliberately slowed back to about 137–144.

The Sambódromo-era samba-enredo follows one poetic form: primeira parte (introduces the story and climbs to a first peak), refrão central (often lyrical), segunda parte, refrão principal (the climax, written 'to fall into the people's mouth'). Some composers add a third refrain; composers keep at least two so the crowd has two things to learn.
The segunda parte is where the bateria rests: dynamics drop, the melody moves lower with longer notes and slower harmonic movement, then the preparation for the main refrain explodes again.
Switching between parallel major and minor keys is now the norm in samba-enredo: in 2015 nine of the twelve Grupo Especial sambas modulated this way, some holding the first key only a few bars.

Functional ii-V-I cycles extended by a VI7 secondary dominant (often altered) are the everyday progression of Brazilian samba and choro accompaniment; Cartola brought tritone substitutions and unusual modulations into samba.

In a roda the low end is the surdo (or pagode's tan-tan) plus the seven-string guitar; on Cartola's 1976 album Dino 7 Cordas, the leading seven-string player of samba and choro, plays alongside a six-string guitar and cavaquinho.

Pagode (late 1970s–80s, Fundo de Quintal) added three sounds: Almir Guineto's four-string banjo, louder than the cavaquinho in a roda; Sereno's hand-played tan-tan holding the samba's main beat; and Ubirany's hand repique for turnarounds.
Samba-enredo is a 'flow genre' whose melody chases the text through the whole story; variety comes from modulation and from the contrast between refrains and verses.
Partido alto sets a fixed refrain sung by everyone against improvised, competitive solo verses, in a major key; pagode lyrics lean on slang, malice and irony.

Outside carnival, sambas are short songs: every track on Cartola's 1976 album runs 2:15–3:53. Bar counts in the form below are a sketch; Prado notes the poetic parts can each hold more than one musical part.

pitfalls.text: Treating beat 1 as the heavy beat. In samba the lowest surdo plays beat 2, the strongest point of the 2/4 bar; beat 1 is the lighter answer.

Pushing the tempo until the syncopation collapses into straight eighths. The 2000s carnival tempos over 150 BPM were an exaggeration schools have since pulled back from; 137–144 is where the recent parades sit.
Confusing samba with bossa nova, baião or Cuban clave. Each has its own accent profile; samba is two pulses over a continuous sixteenth web played by several interlocking voices.

progressions.text: The circular 2-5-1-6: the VI7, often altered, turns back to ii and keeps the cycle going.
The minor 2-5-1 of choro and samba accompaniment, used before the switch to the parallel major.

evidence.inferred: Prado's standard samba-enredo form (first part, central refrain, second part, main refrain) has four distinct sections, and each refrain is sung again when the samba goes round; one pass plus a return of both refrains gives 2 repeats in 6 sections (0.33), several passes push it past 0.5.

summary: Rio de Janeiro's 2/4 song and carnival music: a rolling sixteenth-note web of interlocking percussion over surdos that answer on beat 1 and land hardest on beat 2. Songs are carried by nylon guitars (including the seven-string) and cavaquinho over functional harmony full of secondary dominants and ii-Vs; the carnival samba-enredo is a sung-through story punctuated by refrains.
